cues.text: A King Convenes an Empire-Wide Synod
In June 794, Charlemagne , then at the height of his power over the Frankish realm, summoned bishops from across his territories to a general synod at Frankfurt .

Representatives from England and delegates from the papacy also attended, making the gathering broad enough that some later writers described it as approaching a general council of the Western Church.
Even so, it was never recognized as ecumenical.
Rejecting Nicaea II
One of the council's principal concerns was the Byzantine Second Council of Nicaea (787), which had vindicated the veneration of icons after decades of Eastern iconoclasm.
Working from a badly flawed Latin translation of Nicaea II's acts, Frankfurt's bishops rejected what they took the Eastern council to be teaching.

The translation appeared to command the same worship for images as for God, making their rejection rest on error rather than genuine theological disagreement with the properly understood Eastern position.
The confusion was not fully untangled for some time.
Condemning Adoptionism
Frankfurt also confronted a homegrown Spanish heresy called Adoptionism , associated with Bishop Elipandus of Toledo and Bishop Felix of Urgel.

It taught that Christ, in his human nature, was only the adopted rather than the natural Son of God — a formula the assembled bishops judged to compromise the full, natural sonship at the heart of orthodox Christology.
The council condemned the teaching decisively, and Charlemagne used his own royal authority to press for its suppression throughout his territories.
Royal Authority Over a Church Council

Charlemagne's commanding presence at Frankfurt, and his evident confidence directing the assembled bishops' theological business, reflected a growing entanglement between Frankish royal power and Church governance.
This relationship would only deepen before his imperial coronation in Rome in 800, though Rome occasionally found it uncomfortable while welcoming the council's doctrinal conclusions.
Legacy
Frankfurt's condemnation of Adoptionism helped preserve orthodox Christology across the Carolingian world at a genuine moment of theological confusion.

Its rejection of the mistranslated acts of Nicaea II, later clarified and largely set aside as the confusion was untangled, illustrates how easily even a well-intentioned council's judgment could be distorted by an unreliable text before reaching the wider Church.

Historians of the period regard Frankfurt as a clear preview of the closer, more assertive relationship between crown and Church that would come to define medieval Christendom for centuries afterward.
